questions.question: By default, how does React treat all state updates triggered within one event handler?
options: As equally urgent, which can make an expensive update block a simple one like updating an input
It automatically defers all of them
It only processes the first one
It runs them on a background thread
questions.explanation: Without opting into a transition, every update from an event is treated with the same priority, so a slow render can make even a text input feel laggy.

questions.question: What does wrapping a state update in `startTransition` actually change?
options: It makes the underlying computation run faster
It marks that update as low-priority/interruptible, so React can abandon a stale in-progress render if a newer update arrives
It delays the update by a fixed number of milliseconds
It moves the update to a Web Worker
questions.explanation: Transitions don't speed up the work itself — they change scheduling, letting React interrupt and restart a non-urgent update in favor of something more urgent, like the next keystroke.

questions.question: When should you reach for `useDeferredValue` instead of `useTransition`?
options: When you don't control the state update directly, but have a value (e.g. a prop) you want to let 'lag behind' during expensive renders
They are interchangeable in every situation with no difference
Only when working with CSS animations
questions.explanation: `useTransition` wraps a state update you trigger yourself; `useDeferredValue` wraps a value you've already received and lets a derived render trail behind it.

questions.question: What do concurrent features like `useTransition` NOT do?
options: They don't make the expensive computation itself any faster — filtering 10,000 items still takes the same CPU time
They eliminate the need for keys in lists
questions.explanation: Concurrent rendering changes scheduling/prioritization of renders, not the raw cost of the computation being performed.
